searchText: I was thinking more about interactions between accumulators and epoch-based state eviction. Many witnesses for old epochs will be proofs-of-exclusion. There is an engineering solution to do many proofs-of-exclusion without a witness. A bloom filter returns either "possibly in set" or "definitely not in set". For "possibly in set", we fall back to our static accumulator for that epoch. Bloom filters can be tuned so that their error rate is low. (I know, an engineering solution.) To prevent attacks on bloom filters, we can key the bloom hashes based on the final root hash for that epoch. The bloom filter calculation is a big step (which is bad for blockchain). But this big step has many months to be computed -- it is calculated when the state is still active, but frozen, i.e. the epoch before the current epoch, before it is evicted. Clients will probably just hard-code them anyway. take a look at XOR Filters instead of a bloom filter, might be better https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08258 There is also a Go implementation https://lemire.me/blog/2019/12/19/xor-filters-faster-and-smaller-than-bloom-filters/ I was just looking at xor filters :). I want to keep it simple and say "bloom filters" for now. So that we don't scare anyone away. fair, so I will read "bloom filter" as fast probablistic data structure to exclude the "not in set" cases 😉 Why do you think proof of exclusion will be common? In the current proposal, I guess contract storage all lives at the contracts epoch? If a contract was last touched in epoch M, and you want to resurrect it in epoch N, then the storage in epochs M+1...N-1 at that slot will be empty
